original_question: Do there exist finite-order sporadic Costas arrays of order n > 1 whose dots also form a configuration of non-attacking queens on an n x n chessboard? If such arrays exist, how many are there, and can they be constructed systematically?
target_in_paper: Section 4.3, Problem 7: "Do (sporadic) Costas arrays of finite order n > 1 exist, which also represent configurations of non-attacking queens on an n × n chessboard? If yes, how many are they, and can they be systematically constructed?"
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s exact target. It correctly identifies the finite-order setting, the n > 1 restriction, the non-attacking-queens condition on an n × n board, the relevance of sporadic Costas arrays, and the paper’s two follow-up aims: counting such arrays and asking for a systematic construction.
missing_details: A stand-alone version should define a Costas array/permutation explicitly: a bijection f:[n]→[n] whose distance vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) are all distinct.

A stand-alone version should unpack the queens condition explicitly: because f is a permutation there is one dot in each row and column, and the added requirement is that no two dots share either diagonal direction.

The quantifier should be clarified: the paper asks whether there exists any finite order n > 1 for which such an array exists, and then asks for the total collection/number of all such finite examples.
The paper states a necessary condition that should be made explicit: any finite Costas array with the non-attacking-queens property would have to be sporadic.
The paper is specifically about the finite-order problem; it separately notes that an infinite-array version is already constructible, so that is not part of the target question.
The paper also records an additional scope restriction missing from the draft: there can be only finitely many such finite arrays, via their relation to honeycomb arrays.
No ambient ring, field, homogeneity, or degree data are involved here; the ambient domain is purely combinatorial, namely [n] = {1, ..., n}.
refined_question: Does there exist a finite integer n > 1 and a bijection f:[n]→[n] such that f is a Costas permutation, i.e. all vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) with 1 ≤ j < i ≤ n are distinct, and such that the dot set {(i, f(i)) : i ∈ [n]} forms a configuration of n non-attacking queens on the n × n chessboard, meaning that no two dots lie on a common diagonal in either direction? Since the paper notes that any such finite example would necessarily be sporadic, determine whether any such finite Costas arrays exist; if they do, determine the total number of them and whether they admit a systematic construction.
justification: The draft is essentially a near-verbatim restatement of Problem 7 in Section 4.3. The only real refinements needed to make it fully stand-alone and paper-faithful are to spell out the Costas property using Definition 1, make the chessboard condition explicit in terms of diagonals, and import the nearby contextual restrictions that the paper itself adds: any such finite example must be sporadic, the infinite analogue is already known, and only finitely many finite examples can exist because these are a special case of honeycomb arrays.
